source.version: Conference paper as published in the proceedings of the 26th International Conference on Engineering and Product Design Education (E&PDE 2024, 5-6 September 2024, Aston University); PDF from the Design Society site, footer EPDE2024/1271; all 6 pages read on the PDF
source.title_on_document: EXPLORING CHATGPT'S IMPACT ON STUDENT-TEAM IDEATION OUTCOMES FOR NEW PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT: A PILOT STUDY

supplement.holds: The paper mentions no supplement or appendix.

paper_design_summary: Two sections of a one-day product development class at Brigham Young University, taught one week apart, did two 8-minute team ideation sessions (free and goal-directed association). One section (16 students, 4 teams) used markers and Post-it notes only; the other (19 students, 4 teams) also used ChatGPT 3.5 on a shared team workstation. Two instructors counted each class's ideas, idea categories, and original ideas, reported per student.

studies.label: Pilot: ChatGPT-assisted vs analogue team ideation in two class sections

assignment.what_was_assigned: Whole class section to ChatGPT-assisted or analogue (Post-it only) associative-thinking ideation; one section per condition, sessions one week apart. The paper does not say how sections were allotted to conditions.
assignment.quote: A pilot study was conducted with two sections of a product development class, taught at Brigham Young University (BYU). ... Data was collected from classes taught one week apart.

arms.name: Analogue ideation
arms.description: Students watched 2.5-minute videos on free and goal-directed association, then ideated in teams with markers and Post-it notes, no technology.

arms.name: ChatGPT-assisted ideation
arms.description: Same procedure plus two 1.5-minute ChatGPT demonstration videos; each team used ChatGPT on a computer workstation shown on a wall-mounted television.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusion count is stated. Unclear or incomplete ideas were excluded from the scored outputs (p. 3, Section 2.3.1); less than seven percent of student ideas were excluded, with no exact number stated (pp. 5-6, Section 4.4). The optional post-workshop survey had 30 respondents out of 35 students (15 per class), while Table 1 retains output-analysis denominators of 16 analogue and 19 ChatGPT students (p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2 and Tables 1-3).
participants.who: Undergraduates (first-year to fourth-year) in a product development class at Brigham Young University, USA; about 75 percent engineering majors; 8 teams of 4 or 5 students.
participants.quote: Thirty-five students participated in the study. Sixteen students (4 teams of 4 students each) participated in the class focused on analogue ideation. Nineteen students (3 teams of 5 students and 1 team of 4 students) participated in the ChatGPT-assisted class.
participants.locator: p. 2, Section 2.1 (Participants); counts repeated p. 4, Table 1 (n = 16, n = 19)

ai_tool.how_used: Teams typed prompts into ChatGPT on one shared workstation per team (random word lists, questions about unfamiliar topics, analogous concepts) and wrote ideas on Post-it notes; 60 prompts across both sessions (p. 2, Section 2.2.2; p. 4, Table 4; p. 5, Section 4.3).

task.description: Team ideation of new product ideas for self-identified product problems, using free association then goal-directed association; ideas recorded as sketches and text on Post-it notes.
task.duration: Two 8-minute ideation sessions within a one-day (seven-hour) class (p. 2, Sections 2 and 2.2.1).

contrasts.reported: Table 1, Fluency (ideas per student): Analogue (n = 16) 5.6; ChatGPT (n = 19) 5.1. Class totals of ideas counted by two instructors, divided by students; no SD, test, or p-value.
Table 1, Flexibility (idea groups per student): Analogue (n = 16) 2.8; ChatGPT (n = 19) 2.6. Idea groups from affinity mapping of each team's ideas, divided by students; no SD, test, or p-value.

Table 1, Originality (original ideas per student): Analogue (n = 16) 0.8; ChatGPT (n = 19) 0.4. Count of novel, unexpected, or unique ideas judged by two instructors, divided by students; no SD, test, or p-value.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 2 not met: 35 students analyzed across both arms (16 analogue, 19 ChatGPT; p. 2, Section 2.1 and p. 4, Table 1), well below 50. Criterion 1 not met: the conditions were assigned to two intact class sections taught one week apart, one section per arm, and the paper describes no random assignment (p. 2, Section 2). Criterion 3 met: instructors counted ideas, idea groups, and original ideas on the Post-it outputs. Because the comparison is of intact classes, it fits the observational (quasi_people) context class rather than the small-RCT list; codebook open question 13 decides whether such comparisons appear on the site.

one_line_finding: In a 35-student pilot comparing two class sections, the ChatGPT-assisted section produced slightly fewer ideas (5.1 vs 5.6 per student) and idea groups (2.6 vs 2.8) and half as many original ideas (0.4 vs 0.8) as the analogue section, with no test statistics (p. 4, Table 1).
